2027-05-19.title: Memory of Mar Yaqob Shleeha's first offering of the Holy Qurbono · Wednesday after the Sunday of Pentecost
readings: “Do this in remembrance of me”: the Lord's Supper handed on
“I have eagerly desired to eat this Passover with you”
2027-05-19.alt: Season of Pentecost, the week after the Sunday of Pentecost. The Panchangam keeps today the memory of the first offering of the Holy Qurbono by Mar Yaqob Shleeha. Which James is meant is not stated; our Syriac tradition honours St James, “the Lord's brother” and first bishop of Jerusalem, as the one to whom the Anaphora of St James is ascribed.
2027-05-19.verse: For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord's death until he comes.
theo: Three days after Pentecost our Church keeps a memory that belongs to her very heart: the memory of Mar Yaqob Shleeha offering the Holy Qurbono for the first time. The Panchangam does not say which James is meant, but our Syriac tradition has always looked to St James of Jerusalem, called by St Paul “James the Lord's brother,” that is, a close kinsman of Jesus. The risen Lord appeared to him (1 Corinthians 15:7); he led the Church of Jerusalem and spoke decisively at the council of the apostles (Acts 15:13–21); ancient writers remember him as the first bishop of that city and tell of a man of such prayer that his knees grew hard as a camel's (Hegesippus, in Eusebius, Church History 2.23, in substance). He was put to death in Jerusalem about the year 62. To him the tradition ascribes the Anaphora of St James, the great Eucharistic prayer of the Church of Jerusalem, which became the pattern of the West Syriac Qurbono that we celebrate. We cannot date the morning when he first stood at the altar. But we know what the memory means: from the first days after Pentecost, the Church that had received the Spirit gathered for “the breaking of bread and the prayers” (Acts 2:42), doing what the Lord had commanded.

The Epistle gives us the oldest written account of that command. Writing to Corinth some twenty years after the Resurrection, St Paul says: “For I received from the Lord what I also handed on to you, that the Lord Jesus on the night when he was betrayed took a loaf of bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke it and said, ‘This is my body that is for you. Do this in remembrance of me.’ In the same way he took the cup also, after supper, saying, ‘This cup is the new covenant in my blood. Do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of me.’” Received and handed on: that is how the Qurbono reached us, from the upper room to Jerusalem, from Jerusalem to Antioch, from Antioch to the shores of Kerala, from one generation of priests and faithful to the next. In the Gospel St Luke lets us hear the longing in the Lord's voice: “I have eagerly desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer.” The Supper is not something the disciples arranged for Jesus; it is something he longed to give them. “This is my body, which is given for you.” “This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood.”

St Cyril of Jerusalem, teaching the newly baptised in the very city of St James, told them not to regard the bread and wine as plain bread and wine, for they are the Body and Blood of Christ according to the Lord's own word; even if the senses suggest otherwise, let faith make you sure (Mystagogical Catecheses 4.6, in substance). This is the faith of the Catholic Church: in the Holy Qurbono the one sacrifice of the Cross is made present, and Christ, true God and true man, is truly, really and substantially present under the forms of bread and wine. “Remembrance” here is not a fond memory of something absent; it is the living memorial in which the Lord's sacrifice becomes present to us. And it looks forward too: “For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord's death until he comes.” Today let us thank God for every priest who has stood at the altar for us, from St James to the young priest of our own parish. Let us come to the Qurbono not as spectators but as those whom the Lord eagerly desired to feed. And if we have grown careless, arriving late, leaving early, receiving without preparation, let this memory of the first Qurbono make our next one feel like the first again.
conn: Exodus 24:8 and Luke 22:20: Moses sealed the covenant at Sinai with the blood of sacrifice; Jesus gives the cup of the new covenant in his own blood, as Jeremiah 31:31 had promised.
The pure offering in every place.

Malachi 1:11: from the rising of the sun to its setting a pure offering is made to God's name; from the Didache onward the Church has seen this fulfilled in the Eucharist offered among all the nations.
Exodus 12:14 and Luke 22:15–16: the Passover was a day of remembrance for ever; Jesus eats it with longing and fulfils it in the kingdom of God.
fathers: Do not regard the bread and wine as plain and ordinary, for they are the Body and Blood of Christ, as the Lord himself has declared; though the senses suggest otherwise, let faith establish you (Mystagogical Catecheses 4.6, in substance).

Some keep away from the Eucharist and from prayer because they do not confess that the Eucharist is the flesh of our Saviour Jesus Christ, which suffered for our sins and which the Father raised up (Letter to the Smyrnaeans 7, in substance).

On the Lord's day gather, break bread and give thanks, having first confessed your sins, so that your sacrifice may be pure, as the Lord said: in every place offer me a pure sacrifice (Didache 14, in substance).
magis: The Eucharist is “the source and summit of the Christian life”; all the sacraments and ministries of the Church are bound up with it and directed towards it.
The Eucharist is a sacrifice because it re-presents, makes present, the sacrifice of the Cross, is its memorial and applies its fruit.
In the Most Blessed Sacrament the Body and Blood, together with the soul and divinity, of our Lord Jesus Christ, the whole Christ, is truly, really and substantially contained.

The liturgical traditions in use in the Church include the Latin and the Byzantine, Alexandrian or Coptic, Syriac, Armenian, Maronite and Chaldean rites; the Church holds all of them to be of equal right and dignity.
outline: Ask: when did the Holy Qurbono last feel to me like the first time?
From the upper room through St James to our own altar.
The Lord longs to give himself to us.
The memorial that makes his sacrifice present and looks to his coming.
live: Arrive ten minutes early at your next Holy Qurbono and spend the time in silence before the altar.
Write a short note or say a word of thanks to a priest who has offered the Qurbono for you, and pray for him by name.
2027-05-19.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, on the night you were betrayed you took bread and the cup and gave them to your apostles as your Body and Blood, and you commanded, Do this in remembrance of me. We thank you for Mar Yaqob Shleeha and for all who have offered the Holy Qurbono from the first days of your Church until now. As you eagerly desired to eat the Passover with your disciples, give us a hunger for your holy Mysteries. Make us worthy to receive them with faith and love, to proclaim your death and Resurrection, and to wait for your coming in glory. With your Father and your Holy Spirit, now and for ever. Amen.
altar: Today the altar itself is the feast. What Mar Yaqob offered in Jerusalem, our priest offers in our parish: the one sacrifice of Christ, made present for us until he comes.

quick: Our Church remembers today the first offering of the Holy Qurbono by Mar Yaqob Shleeha; tradition honours St James of Jerusalem, to whom the Anaphora of St James is ascribed.
St Paul hands on what he received: the Lord's words over the bread and the cup, “Do this in remembrance of me.”
In Luke the Lord says, “I have eagerly desired to eat this Passover with you”: the Qurbono is his longing to give himself to us.
2027-05-19.action: Come early to your next Holy Qurbono and prepare in silence.
2027-05-19.question: Do I come to the Qurbono as one whom the Lord eagerly desired to feed?
term: The Syriac word for offering or sacrifice, from a root meaning to draw near. The Holy Qurbono is the Eucharistic sacrifice, in which we draw near to God through the offering of Christ.
kidsaint: St James, the man with camel knees

St James was a relative of Jesus and became the first bishop of Jerusalem. An old writer says he prayed on his knees so much that his knees became hard like a camel's! Our Church remembers that he offered the Holy Qurbono, and the prayer of our Qurbono is called by his name. Lesson: when you kneel and pray, you are doing what St James did.

family.explain: At the Last Supper Jesus took bread and said, This is my body, which is given for you. Then he took the cup and said, This cup is the new covenant in my blood. He told his friends to do this to remember him. Today our Church remembers St James, who offered the Holy Qurbono in Jerusalem long ago. Every time our priest offers the Qurbono, Jesus gives himself to us in the same way.
family.intention: We pray for our priests, and for children preparing for their First Holy Communion.
family.ask: Ask: “How can we get ready as a family for the next Qurbono?”

illus: A young priest was posted to a small mission station in the hills of Idukki, where only eleven families came to the Qurbono. In his first month he felt that his years of study were wasted on so few. One morning an old man who had walked an hour in the rain stayed behind after the Qurbono and said: Achen, for thirty years we had the Qurbono here only once a month; now we have it every day. I prayed for this before you were born. The priest went back to the altar after the man had left and knelt there for a long time. He said later that it was the day he learned that no Qurbono is small.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, you longed to share the Passover with your disciples. Give us a longing for your holy Mysteries. Amen.
share: I received from the Lord what I also handed on to you (1 Corinthians 11:23). Who handed on the faith of the Qurbono to me?
I have eagerly desired to eat this Passover with you (Luke 22:15). How do I prepare to meet the Lord who longs for me?
You proclaim the Lord's death until he comes (1 Corinthians 11:26). What does my life proclaim after the Qurbono?
pm.resp: Lord, make us worthy of your holy Mysteries.
interc: For all bishops and priests, that they may offer the Holy Qurbono with faith and reverence.
For those who have stopped coming to the Qurbono, that they may hunger for it again.
For children preparing for First Holy Communion and for their families.
For Christians who cannot attend the Qurbono because of persecution, distance or illness.
For our parish, that the Qurbono may be the centre of our life.
pm.close: Father, through Mar Yaqob Shleeha and the apostles you handed on to your Church the holy Mysteries of the Body and Blood of your Son. Keep us faithful to them, make us long for them, and through them prepare us for the wedding feast of the Lamb. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, today our Church remembers Mar Yaqob Shleeha offering the Holy Qurbono for the first time. Our tradition honours St James of Jerusalem, the Lord's brother, the first bishop of that city, to whom the Anaphora of St James is ascribed, the source of the Qurbono we celebrate. After Pentecost the first Christians devoted themselves to the breaking of bread and the prayers (Acts 2:42).

St Paul tells us how the Qurbono came to us: For I received from the Lord what I also handed on to you (1 Corinthians 11:23). On the night when he was betrayed, the Lord took bread and said, This is my body that is for you. Do this in remembrance of me (1 Corinthians 11:24). From the upper room, through St James and the apostles, through the centuries, this gift has been handed on to our own altar.

In the Gospel we hear the longing of Jesus: I have eagerly desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer (Luke 22:15). He gives the bread and says, This is my body, which is given for you; he gives the cup, the new covenant in my blood (Luke 22:19–20). What we receive is not a symbol only. It is truly his Body and his Blood, his one sacrifice made present.

For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord's death until he comes (1 Corinthians 11:26). Let us thank God today for every priest who has offered the Qurbono for us. Let us come early, prepare our hearts, and receive the Lord as one who longs to feed us. Amen.
kids: Children, do you know what the Holy Qurbono is? It is the greatest gift Jesus gave us. At the Last Supper he said: This is my body, this is my blood, do this in memory of me. Today we remember St James, who offered the Qurbono in Jerusalem long, long ago. He prayed so much that his knees became hard! Next time you go to the Qurbono, remember: Jesus really comes to us, and he is very happy to see you.

intro: Theme: “Do this in remembrance of me.”
On the memory of Mar Yaqob Shleeha's first offering of the Holy Qurbono: what was received and handed on, the Lord's longing, and the memorial that waits for his coming.

sub: The oldest account of the Supper.
q: This day shall be a day of remembrance for you.
They devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers.
points.apply: Learn by heart one response of the Holy Qurbono that you usually only mumble, and say it with meaning next time.

sub: The Lord longs to give himself.
Truly present, not a symbol only.

points.apply: Make a short visit to the church this week and spend ten minutes before the Lord in the tabernacle.

points.apply: After your next Qurbono, do one concrete act of love the same day, so that your life proclaims what you received.

concl: What Mar Yaqob offered in Jerusalem, the Church still offers: the one sacrifice of Christ, received and handed on.
The Lord who eagerly desired to eat the Passover with his disciples still longs to feed us, until he comes.
2027-05-19.resolve: Come to the Holy Qurbono prepared and hungry, thank God for our priests, and let your life proclaim the Lord's death and Resurrection.
